statement: Every Danish noun has four forms — indefinite and definite, singular and plural (bil, bilen, biler, bilerne) — and the sentence decides which one you need.
explanation: Use the indefinite singular after en/et, and remember that possessives (min, vores, Peters) always take the bare form without an ending. Use the definite (-en/-et, -ne) when the listener knows which one you mean, e.g. it was mentioned before or a relative clause points it out. Numbers and words like mange/flere need the plural. Learn the irregular plurals (barn – børn, mand – mænd, bog – bøger, øje – øjne). The classic trap is adding a definite ending after a possessive: min bil, not *min bilen.

examples.note: After a possessive the noun has no definite ending.

examples.right: Vi har tre børn. Børnene går i skole.
examples.note: Plural after a number; definite plural once we know which children.
barn has an irregular plural: børn, børnene.

da: Generel form eller ubestemt form – ental
en: General (no article) vs indefinite form — singular
statement: Use the bare noun with no article for a substance, an activity, a profession or a fixed expression, and en/et + noun for one countable individual thing.
explanation: Danish leaves out the article when a noun names a substance or something in general (Jeg spiser fisk, Jeg drikker kaffe), a job or role after være/blive (Han er læge), and in fixed verb phrases (spille fodbold, køre bil, have feber, gå i skole). Use en/et when you mean one concrete, countable thing (Der svømmer en fisk i akvariet) or when the profession noun has an adjective or a relative clause describing the person (Han er en dygtig læge). The typical trap is copying English: *Hun er en sygeplejerske.

examples.note: With an adjective the article comes back.

examples.right: Jeg spiser fisk. / Jeg fangede en fisk.
examples.note: Fish as food (substance) vs one fish (countable).

da: Generel form eller ubestemt form – flertal
statement: When you talk about a kind of thing in general, use the plural without an article (Jeg kan godt lide katte); use en/et + singular only for one individual.
explanation: Statements about likes, fears, hobbies, jobs and categories use the indefinite plural: Hun er bange for hunde, Han samler på frimærker, Hun reparerer biler. Use en/et + singular when you mean one particular (or one single) thing, often shown by den/det later in the text. Mass nouns such as rugbrød, mælk, kaffe have no such plural and stay in the bare singular. The learner trap is using the singular for a whole category (*Jeg kan godt lide en kat).

examples.wrong: Jeg er bange for en hund.
examples.note: A general fear of the whole category: plural, no article.

examples.right: Vi har en hund. Den hedder Max.

examples.note: Mass noun: bare singular, no plural.

statement: Use the indefinite form (en/et) for something new to the listener and the definite form (-en/-et/-ne) for something the listener can identify.
explanation: First mention is usually indefinite (Jeg har fået et brev); the next mention is definite (Brevet er fra kommunen). Things that are unique (solen), part of something already mentioned (et hus … haven), or pointed out by a following relative clause (filmen, du så) are definite. Several fixed phrases are definite too: ondt i hovedet, tre dage om ugen. Be careful: a relative clause that only describes does not make the noun definite (De har en søn, der hedder Max).

examples.right: Jeg har købt en lejlighed. Lejligheden har tre værelser.
examples.note: New information first, known information second.

examples.wrong: Jeg har ondt i et hoved.
examples.note: Your own body parts are definite.

examples.wrong: Jeg arbejder tre dage om en uge.
examples.right: Jeg arbejder tre dage om ugen.
examples.note: Fixed phrase: om ugen, om året.
